questions.cardText:
[Ecology] What triggers the seasonal color change in snowshoe hares?
A. Availability of food
B. Daylight length
C. Temperature change
Answer: B. Snowshoe hares switch from brown to white based on daylight length. However, with earlier winters due to global climate change, they often appear mismatched against melting snow. This out-of-sync color change increases their visibility to predators, negatively affecting their survival.
questions.de: Was löst beim Schneeschuhhasen den jahreszeitlichen Fellwechsel von Braun zu Weiß aus?
questions.en: What triggers the snowshoe hare's seasonal coat change from brown to white?

timeline.labelEn: Johann Erxleben first describes the snowshoe hare, Lepus americanus
timeline.labelDe: Johann Erxleben beschreibt den Schneeschuhhasen (Lepus americanus) erstmals

source.title: Lynx and Snowshoe Hare: The Color of Survival

questions.notes: Confirmed: 'It is this changing photoperiod … that triggers the molt' (Defenders of Wildlife); snow cover sets only the pace. Card's explanation slightly garbled: the mismatch comes from shorter snow seasons (later snowfall, earlier melt), not 'earlier winters'. Timeline (species description 1777) from Wikipedia 'Snowshoe hare'.

questions.cardText:
[Art History] “Vanitas” paintings in art symbolize:
A. Political power and strength
B. The transience of life and the futility of pleasure
C. Religious devotion and purity
Answer: B.
questions.de: Wofür stehen Vanitas-Gemälde, die Stillleben mit Totenschädeln und verlöschenden Kerzen?
questions.en: What do vanitas paintings, the still lifes of skulls and guttering candles, symbolize?
questions.answerDe: Die Vergänglichkeit des Lebens und die Nichtigkeit der Freuden
questions.answerEn: The transience of life and the futility of pleasure

timeline.labelEn: Vanitas painting flourishes, above all among Dutch painters of the 17th century
timeline.labelDe: Die Vanitas-Malerei blüht, vor allem bei niederländischen Malern des 17. Jahrhunderts

questions.notes: Confirmed: a memento-mori genre symbolizing the transience of life, the uselessness of pleasure and the certainty of death (Wikipedia); genre spans the 16th–17th centuries.
